blocks.en: My boss was yelling at me yesterday, and I told him to back off.
blocks.def: back off = to move backwards away from someone, usually because you are frightened
blocks.back: In this situation your boss is angry at you and he's kind of getting in your face a little bit, and you want him to move back a little bit, so you may just say: Hey, Boss. Back off! You're coming on a little too strong.

blocks.en: The dog started barking at me when I entered the yard, so I backed off.
blocks.def: back off = to move backwards away from someone, usually because you are frightened
blocks.back: There's a reversal motion here. You're going along, you walk into a yard and suddenly you'll hear this dog barking and you back off, you leave the yard. Because you don't want the dog to bite you.

blocks.en: In order to lose weight, I have decided to back off of the desserts for a little while.
blocks.def: back off = to decrease the intensity or amount of something:
blocks.back: So, I'm somebody who loves my cake and ice cream and maybe I need to just, you know, to decrease the number of calories I'm consuming. I may need to back off from the desserts.

blocks.en: Another boss might have told the editor to back off and not pursue the story.
blocks.def: back off = to draw back from doing something
blocks.back: A different boss might have been concerned that pursuing the story could have negative consequences; the suggestion is that he might therefore have asked the editor to turn away from the investigation and have no further involvement with this line of enquiry.

blocks.en: Back off and let me make my own decisions.
blocks.def: back off = to stop interfering
blocks.back: Although "back off" can mean "physically draw back", very often, as here, it has an entirely metaphorical force, meaning "stop interfering" / "leave me alone".

blocks.en: He refused to back off from his earlier statement.
blocks.def: to back off from = to withdraw from or stop defending a previous statement. This sense of
blocks.back: "back off" is specific to US English usage; in UK English the verb would be "back down". One person is asking another to accept that something they have said was wrong, and to admit their error, but the other person is unwilling to do this.

blocks.en: I'm really feisty and I never back down from a confrontation.
blocks.def: back down = to admit you were wrong, or to stop supporting a position
blocks.back: I often think of backing down in the context of a confrontation, you've got one person over here and you have another person over here and they're butting heads. Eventually, one of them is going to have to back down if the confrontation is going to be resolved.

blocks.en: When I challenged my neighbor on his plans to build a fence between our houses he backed down.
blocks.def: back down = to withdraw from a position, opinion, or commitment
blocks.back: So, in this instance maybe I had a neighbor who wanted to put a fence and he didn't really care what my opinion was, so I maybe heard about it from somebody else that he was planning on putting this fence in between my yard and his yard, and I don't want that fence, and he probably needed to consult me first before going ahead with his plans, and in any event I don't want the fence so I confronted him and he backed down from that.

blocks.en: Neither the airline nor the pilots are willing to back down, so the strike will continue for a while longer.
blocks.def: back down = to withdraw from a position, opinion, or commitment
blocks.back: I know that in Brazil as in The United States strikes often occur. Maybe university professors don't think they're getting enough pay, or maybe the letter carriers feel that they don't have enough benefits and so they'll go on strike. And they have their set of demands, the workers have their set of demands and the company or a management has their set of set of plans. And sometimes that's also a confrontational situation in which they need to come to an agreement, and if neither of them back down from whatever their demands are, the strike will continue, indefinitely.

blocks.en: Neither side is willing to back down.
blocks.def: back down = to accept something you previously stated was wrong, and admit it.
blocks.back: In this example, two different opinions or perspectives are represented by two parties, and both refuse to change their position in the face of counter arguments.

blocks.en: Eventually, Roberto backed down and apologized.
blocks.def: back down = to accept something you previously stated was wrong, and admit it.
blocks.back: In this example, Roberto had previously stated something which he now considers incorrect, so he states something contrary to his previous statement, admitting he was wrong.

blocks.en: Jane backed down from her position on the budget.
blocks.def: back down = to accept something you previously stated was wrong, and admit it.
blocks.back: In this example, Jane has changed her mind regarding the budget, and admits it.

blocks.en: James tried to start a fight with Henry, but Henry backed down when the police arrived.
blocks.def: back down = to no longer assert yourself / to no longer insist on doing something
blocks.back: Perhaps Henry wanted to respond violently, but when the police arrived he decided that would be unwise, controlled himself, and no longer acted as if he wanted to retaliate.

blocks.en: I will never give up on my dream to attain fluency in Portuguese.
blocks.def: give up = to stop doing something that you are trying hard to do
blocks.back: So in this case I have an objective, a goal and I'm going to have some obstacles, it's going to be difficult, I'm going to get bored, it's going to get tiring. So, I am just not going to give up on that dream, I'm going to continue ahead.

blocks.en: A fierce competitor will never give up in the heat of battle.
blocks.def: give up = to stop doing something that you are trying hard to do
blocks.back: Again, this has to do with just, in spite of all obstacles just moving forward and never giving up. We talk a lot about this spirit of not wanting to give up in athletics. The best competitors, the best athletes, are those that will never give up, no matter how injured they are, no matter how tough the competition is, they are just determined to continue ahead and never give up.

blocks.en: I have been addicted to cigarettes for fifteen years and I'm finding it very difficult to give up smoking.
blocks.def: give up = to stop doing something that you do regularly
blocks.back: So in this case, it would be a positive thing if the person would give up this particular bad habit. A lot of us have bad habits that we should give up, maybe we eat too much, maybe we smoke or drink too much, maybe we spend too much time watching television. So, these are instances in which giving up is letting go and surrendering a habit or a behavior that is not beneficial for us.

blocks.en: I give up - tell me the answer!
blocks.def: give up = to stop trying / to admit you cannot do something
blocks.back: Someone has tried to find the answer to a question that they have been asked, but they now admit that they do not know the answer. 'I give up' therefore means 'I no longer want to try'.

blocks.en: They were forced to give up their home because they couldn't pay the mortgage.
blocks.def: give (something) up = To no longer hold onto something that you would rather keep
blocks.back: As these people were no longer able to make the required payments, they had to accept that they could not keep their home (and they therefore had to relinquish ownership).

blocks.en: I've given up trying to help her.
blocks.def: give up = to stop trying / to admit you cannot do something
blocks.back: Someone has been trying to help this woman, but for some reason they are no longer willing to try.

blocks.en: Most people gave up on him when he quit school, but he went back and earned his degree two years later.
blocks.def: give up on (someone) = to no longer have faith or belief in (someone)
blocks.back: Most people lost their belief that this person could achieve something positive when he left school. The implication is that people had come to believe that the person who left school would not benefit from any assistance or encouragement, as it would not make any difference to the student's attitude (or perceived lack of ability, perhaps).

blocks.en: ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE This is Brooks Gillespie talking to you from Omaha, Nebraska.
And, in today's lesson we're going to talk about three different phrasal verbs: back off, back down and give up.
And I think before we start talking about the different verbs and some of the sample sentences, we need to talk about the word Back.
Because the word back is in these verbs, and, so there's a sense of motion.
This is my front, and this is my back.
So, whenever we're backing or we're backing up or backing off, we're...we're doing a reverse motion.
A common expression in the English language where we hear the word back is back and forth.
If I'm rocking I'm rocking back and forth, back and forth.
So when we use the word back, we're talking about a reverse motion.
And what I've done here is I've written three sentences using each of these phrasal verbs to give you an idea of how they are used in different situations.
The first phrasal verb we're going to talk about is back off.
And, when somebody is backing off, there's a reverse motion, either literally or figuratively.

For instance, if I was driving my car and I pulled up on the curb and the front wheel was upon the curb, I would have to back off of the curb, so that the wheel would come down, so that I could properly park.
What I'm going to do is read you a sentence and then explain to you how the verb works in that particular sentence.
The first sentence is: My boss was yelling at me yesterday, and I told him to back off.
In this situation your boss is angry at you and he's kind of getting in your face a little bit, and you want him to move back a little bit, so you may just say: Hey, Boss.
You're coming on a little too strong.
The second sentence is: The dog started barking at me when I entered the yard, so I backed off.
Again, there's a reversal motion here.
You're going along, you walk into a yard and suddenly "auauauaua" you'll hear this dog barking and you back off, you leave the yard.
Because you don't want the dog to bite you.
And our third sentence is: In order to lose weight, I have decided to back off of the desserts for a little while.
So, I'm somebody who loves my cake and ice cream and maybe I need to just, you know, to decrease the number of calories I'm consuming.
I may need to back off from the desserts.
Our next phrasal verb is back down.
Slightly different, it has to do with retreat or surrender, in a certain sense.
And the first sentence I came up with is: I'm really feisty and I never back down from a confrontation.
I often think of backing down in the context of a confrontation, you've got one person over here and you have another person over here and they're butting heads.
Eventually, one of them is going to have to back down if the confrontation is going to be resolved.
My second sentence for back down: When I challenged my neighbor on his plans to build a fence between our houses he backed down.

So, in this instance maybe I had a neighbor who wanted to put a fence and he didn't really care what my opinion was, so I maybe heard about it from somebody else that he was planning on putting this fence in between my yard and his yard, and I don't want that fence, and he probably needed to consult me first before going ahead with his plans, and in any event I don't want the fence so I confronted him and he backed down from that.
And my third example of back down is: Neither the airline nor the pilots are willing to back down, so the strike will continue for a while longer.
I know that in Brazil as in The United States strikes often occur.
Maybe university professors don't think they're getting enough pay, or maybe the letter carriers feel that they don't have enough benefits and so they'll go on strike.
And they have their set of demands, the workers have their set of demands and the company or a management has their set of set of plans.

And sometimes that's also a confrontational situation in which they need to come to an agreement, and if neither of them back down from whatever their demands are, the strike will continue, indefinitely.
Alright, now the third phrasal verb that we're going to discuss is give up.
And this is definitely a situation where you just, you let go, you're defeated, you stop fighting.
The first sentence that I came up with is: I will never give up on my dream to attain fluency in Portuguese.
So in this case I have an objective, a goal and I'm going to have some obstacles, it's going to be difficult, I'm going to get bored, it's going to get tiring.
So, I am just not going to give up on that dream, I'm going to continue ahead.
A fierce competitor will never give up in the heat of battle.
Again, this has to do with just, in spite of all obstacles just moving forward and never giving up.
We talk a lot about this spirit of not wanting to give up in athletics.

The best competitors, the best athletes, are those that will never give up, no matter how injured they are, no matter how tough the competition is, they are just determined to continue ahead and never give up.
And my third example is: I have been addicted to cigarettes for fifteen years and I'm finding it very difficult to give up smoking.
So in this case, it would be a positive thing if the person would give up this particular bad habit.
A lot of us have bad habits that we should give up, maybe we eat too much, maybe we smoke or drink too much, maybe we spend too much time watching television.
So, these are instances in which giving up is letting go and surrendering a habit or a behavior that is not beneficial for us.
So, I hope these examples have helped you and looking forward to more opportunities to discuss phrasal verbs with you.

blocks.en: Playing on the competitive soccer team was hard, but Sharon wanted to follow through with the season.
blocks.def: Follow through = to keep going in an activity till it finishes.
blocks.back: Sharon is playing on a soccer team that is competitive, or where all the players are maybe much better than she is. Because it's hard, she has thought about quitting, but instead, she decides to follow through, or finish, playing the whole season.

blocks.en: Kayla has not followed through on any of the art projects that she started in class this school year.
blocks.def: Follow through = to keep going in an activity till it finishes.
blocks.back: We know from the sentence that Kayla has started many art projects this year, but we can tell that she has not finished any of them. Kayla has not followed through or completed any of the art projects that she has started this year.

blocks.en: John was happy that his brother could follow through on his promise to pay him back for the $1,000 that he loaned.
blocks.def: Follow through = to keep going in an activity till it finishes.
blocks.back: John loaned his brother some money and thought that his brother would pay him back since he gave a promise. John was happy that his brother completed, or followed through on his promise by paying him back $1,000.

blocks.en: If you don't follow through with your bat, you might not hit the ball as hard as you wanted to.
blocks.def: Follow through = to continue a motion until it is complete
blocks.back: When someone is playing baseball they hope to hit the ball as hard as they can. If you don't complete the motion, or follow through with your swing, you won't be able to hit the ball are hard.

blocks.en: Jorge was going to marry Giselle in just 2 weeks, but decided he couldn't follow through with the wedding because he didn't love her.
blocks.def: Follow through = to keep going in an activity till it finishes.
blocks.back: When someone decides not to follow through with a wedding, they are decided not to get married. They decide to cancel the wedding before it happens, in this case it is because they are not in love with the other person.

blocks.en: I had the choice to follow through with the language course if I paid a fee, but I couldn't afford it.
blocks.def: Follow through = to keep going in an activity till it finishes.
blocks.back: The language course had a fee, or payment, in order to participate. In this case, the participant didn't have the money, so they were not able to follow through, or complete, the language course.

blocks.en: Sally went bowling with her family and accidentally dropped the bowling ball on her foot because she didn't follow through.
blocks.def: Follow through = to continue a motion until it is complete
blocks.back: When bowling, in order to complete the motion and get the ball to go down the lane, one must follow through. Because Sally did not complete the motion, or follow through, the ball did not go down the lane and instead dropped on her foot.

blocks.en: We were not able to follow through with our plans to go surfing because the weather was so bad.
blocks.def: Follow through = to keep going in an activity till it finishes.
blocks.back: In this case, they had a plan to go surfing, but because the weather was bad, they were not able to complete their plan. They couldn't follow through with surfing because of the weather.

blocks.en: When her computer battery died, Cathy was not able to follow through with the purchase she was making online.
blocks.def: Follow through = to keep going in an activity till it finishes.
blocks.back: Cathy wanted to purchase something online, but she was not able to finish her purchase because her computer battery died. She wasn't able to follow through with the purchase.

blocks.en: After it rained all day, Kyle knew that his outdoor birthday party wasn't going to turn out the way he hoped it would.
blocks.def: Turn out = for something to happen the way you expected it to.
blocks.back: Kyle had expected to have a great birthday party outdoors, but because it rained, we know that the birthday party is probably cancelled, or moved inside. So the party didn't turn out the way Kyle thought it would.

blocks.en: When the wedding was over, Justine felt like everything turned out much better her mother said it would.
blocks.def: Turn out = for something to happen the way you expected it to.
blocks.back: At a wedding, there are many things that need to happen in order for the day to go smoothly. Justine felt like everything happen better than she expected, and the wedding turned out nicely.

blocks.en: Jamie and Sam only invited 25 people to their house to watch the game, but 50 people turned out!
blocks.def: Turn out = to be present at or to come to an event or activity
blocks.back: In this case, there are people coming to watch a game at Jamie and Sam's house. 50 people came, or turned out, to watch the game.

blocks.en: Ximena was scared when her father turned out the lights in their camping tent.
blocks.def: Turn out = to cause the lights to go off
blocks.back: When camping outdoors, it can be very dark at night. We can imagine that when the lights go off, or are turned out, that someone might become scared because they can no longer see what's near them.

blocks.en: Mrs. Allen used two cups of sugar instead of one cup of sugar, so the cake turned out much sweeter than it was supposed to.
blocks.def: Turn out = for something to happen the way you expected it to.
blocks.back: In this case, Mrs. Allen used twice as much sugar as she was supposed to. That means that final cake was too sweet - it turned out much too sweet!

blocks.en: To help them students see the screen better, the professor turned out the lights that were shining in their eyes.
blocks.def: Turn out = to cause the lights to go off
blocks.back: When the students were trying to look at the screen, the light was shining too brightly in their eyes. To solve this problem, the professor turned out, or shut off the lights.

blocks.en: When the flyer said, "Free Pizza!", over 200 students turned out to the academic meeting.
blocks.def: Turn out = to be present at or to come to an event or activity
blocks.back: The flyer that said, "Free Pizza!" was exciting to many students. Because of this, many students were present at the academic meeting.

blocks.en: Cancelling the baseball game turned out to be a bad idea, as the storm was gone before the game even started.
blocks.def: Turn out = for something to happen the way you expected it to.
blocks.back: The baseball game was cancelled because there was going to be a storm. However, the storm was gone before the game started, so it was not a good idea to cancel the game. It turned out to be a bad idea to cancel the game.

blocks.en: Only 3 people turned out for the 7:30am meeting that Mr. Alvarez held on Monday morning.
blocks.def: Turn out = to be present at or to come to an event or activity
blocks.back: Mr. Alvarez had a meeting scheduled for 7:30am on a Monday morning. Not many people want to get up for a meeting at 7:30am on a Monday morning, so only 3 people came, or turned out.

blocks.en: Even though she was nice, Ashley turned out to be a bad friend because she never called Jenny back.
blocks.def: Turn out = for something to happen the way you expected it to.
blocks.back: Jenny thought that Ashley was going to be a good friend because she was nice. However, Ashley didn't ever call Jenny back, so Jenny decided she was not a good friend. It turned out that Ashley was not a good friend.

blocks.en: Calem decided to go through with the airplane trip to Hawaii even though he didn't like flying.
blocks.def: Go through with = to do something even if there are problems or concerns
blocks.back: Calem is going a trip to Hawaii and he is travelling by airplane. Calem does not like flying on planes, but is going to do it because he is excited about going to Hawaii.

blocks.en: Even though she is nervous, Janie decided to go through with the performance on stage because she signed up two months ago.
blocks.def: Go through with = to complete a task or event that your promised to do
blocks.back: Janie signed up for the performance two months ago. Now she is feeling nervous to perform on stage, but feels like she needs to since she signed up so long ago. While she is nervous, she is going through with the performance anyways.

blocks.en: Yessica was right in the middle of a terrible headache, but had to go through with the weekly meeting in her boss' office.
blocks.def: Go through with = to complete a task or event that your promised to do
blocks.back: Yessica is having a terrible headache, and probably wants to sit down and rest for a bit. However, she has already promised to meet with her boss, and has to go through with the meeting while she has a bad headache.

blocks.en: Carrie didn't think she liked Jake at all, but decided to go through with the dinner date because he was a nice guy.
blocks.def: Go through with = to complete a task or event that your promised to do
blocks.back: Carrie promised to go on a date with Jake. After she made the promise, she decided that she didn't really like him that much. Because she thinks he is nice, and she doesn't want to be rude, she decides to go through with the date.

blocks.en: Mr. Klein found out that the company he was meeting with was in financial trouble, but decided to go through with the interview anyways.
blocks.def: Go through with = to do something even if there are problems or concerns
blocks.back: If a company is in financial trouble, they may not have enough money to pay a new employee. Mr. Klein is worried that this company will not be able to pay him if he is hired. He decides to go through with the interview even though he is concerned.

blocks.en: Hannah's father thinks she should not go through with the wedding because her fiancé has never had a job, and doesn't want a job.
blocks.def: Go through with = to do something even if there are problems or concerns
blocks.back: Hannah's father probably thinks that her fiancé is lazy, mainly because he doesn't have a job, and does not want a job. Her father probably thinks he will be a bad husband. He thinks she should not get married to him, and should not go through with the wedding.

blocks.en: Jamal couldn't go through with his trip to Chile in July because he wasn't able to save enough money.
blocks.def: Go through with = to do something even if there are problems or concerns
blocks.back: It can often be expensive to travel, and Jamal was saving money so that he could go to Chile. Because he didn't save enough money, he did not have enough money plane ticket, or other costs, and couldn't go on the trip.

blocks.en: The art department at the elementary school could not go through with the summer camp because only 1 student signed up.
blocks.def: Go through with = to complete a task or event that your promised to do
blocks.back: The art department was going to have a summer camp, but only 1 student showed up. The art department probably thought it was not worth it to have a camp with only 1 student, so they decided not to have, or go through with, the summer camp.

blocks.en: Haley couldn't go through with the cake recipe for the party because she didn't have the right ingredients.
blocks.def: Haley had promised to make a cake for the party. In order to make a cake, you need the right
blocks.back: ingredients. Because Haley didn't have the right ingredients she was not able to make, or go through with, the cake recipe.

blocks.en: The new company decided they could not go through with their updated business plan until they had hired a new CEO.
blocks.def: Go through with = to do something even if there are problems or concerns
blocks.back: The new company wanted to start their new business plan. They decided that before they could do that they needed to hired a new CEO. They were not able to start, or go through with, their new business plan until they hired a new CEO.

audios.file: AUDIO Lesson 04.mp3
audios.label: Narração

blocks.en: Every Sunday, I dig out the old fruits and vegetables from my refrigerator.
blocks.def: dig out = to remove something or someone
blocks.back: Some of the foods in my refrigerator may be going rotten, and I need to throw them away.

blocks.en: Charles is planning on digging out the weeds that are infesting his flower beds this month.
blocks.def: dig out = to remove something or someone
blocks.back: In this example, Charles wants to improve the appearance of his flower beds, so he is going to pull out the uninvited plants.

blocks.en: Macy is trying to dig out the splinter in her finger.
blocks.def: dig out = to remove something or someone
blocks.back: In this case, Macy is working to remove whatever is stuck in her finger.

blocks.en: The rescue team is doing their best to dig out any survivors beneath the avalanche.
blocks.def: dig out = to remove something or someone
blocks.back: In this case, a group of mountain climbers are buried under an avalanche. A rescue team is trying to retrieve anyone who is still alive under the snow.

blocks.en: The lifeguard jumped in the swimming pool to dig out the poor boy who had trouble swimming.
Tom and I are both going to chip in on our restaurant bill.
blocks.def: chip in = to contribute some money
blocks.back: In this example, two people are deciding to split the price of their food at a restaurant. dig out = to remove something or someone Even though the act of digging is more commonly used to describe the act of rummaging through items such as dirt, sand, or snow, it can also be used to describe removing things from water.

blocks.en: Sheila paid for most of her school expenses, but she asked her parents to chip in too.
blocks.def: chip in = to contribute some money
blocks.back: Sheila is trying to pay for her education but needs a little help. She asks her parents to help support her.

blocks.en: All of us chipped in to buy Jamie a birthday gift.
blocks.def: chip in = to contribute some money
blocks.back: In this example, a group of people are donating money to buy their friend Jamie a present.

blocks.en: Our teacher said we can have a pizza party if our whole class will chip in to pay for the pizzas.
blocks.def: chip in = to contribute some money
blocks.back: A class of students wants to have a party, and the teacher will allow it if the students pay for it themselves.

blocks.en: If I chip in for this month's rent, can I stay at your apartment?
I would like to chip in on this topic.
blocks.def: chip in = to contribute to a discussion
blocks.back: Imagine a group of people are having a discussion. You might have something to add to the conversation, and this is a good way to let that be known.

blocks.en: During the debate, the debaters argued furiously and chipped in even when it wasn't their turn to speak.
blocks.def: chip in = to contribute to a discussion
blocks.back: In this case, there is a political debate on television where the debaters are constantly inter-rupting each other. chip in = to contribute some money In this case, I need a place to stay for a while and have a good friend who might let me live with him / her if I help pay the rent.

blocks.en: The student chipped in and shared his thoughts during the history lesson.
blocks.def: chip in = contribute to a discussion
blocks.back: This example shows a case where a student gives their opinion during a teacher's lecture.

blocks.en: I wanted to chip in, but I held my tongue.
blocks.def: chip in = to contribute to a discussion
blocks.back: Even when you have something to chip in, you don't always say it.

blocks.en: I could barely deliver my speech, because the audience chipped in every few minutes.
blocks.def: chip in = to contribute to a discussion
blocks.back: In this example, I had to keep stopping and starting during a speech because the crowd kept interrupting me.

blocks.en: I hope our company's sales pick up this year.
blocks.def: pick up = to improve
blocks.back: Here, a business is hoping their sales begin to increase.

blocks.en: The wind speed picked up while the boaters were out at sea.
blocks.def: pick up = to improve, to increase.
blocks.back: In the example, the speaker is expressing that something started to move faster. The wind, a car, or even a runner can pick up speed.

blocks.en: Katie picked up English really quickly.
blocks.def: pick up = to learn quickly
blocks.back: In this case, Katie became fluent in English in a very short amount of time.

blocks.en: I picked up on the dog's hint to leave him alone.
blocks.def: pick up = to learn quickly
blocks.back: People and animal's body language give clues as to what they are thinking, and you might be able to decipher this sometimes.

blocks.en: I have a package I need to pick up from the post office.
Jake picked up his phone after he dropped it on the floor.
blocks.def: pick up = to collect
blocks.back: When you use your hand to raise an item off of a surface, you are picking it up.

blocks.en: The cabin TV's satellite will not pick up Channel 3.
blocks.def: pick up = to receive (a broadcast)
blocks.back: In this case, a television is not able to display Channel 3 due to bad reception.

blocks.en: I can't call the doctor because I can't pick up any cell phone signal in this area.
blocks.def: pick up = to receive (a broadcast)
blocks.back: In this case, I can't make telephone calls on my mobile phone due to bad signal.

blocks.en: I have to pick up my brother from the barber shop on my way home from the grocery store.
blocks.def: pick up = to collect (a person). This differs from the 'collect a thing' meaning - as that means
blocks.back: 'collect and bring back' whereas this means either (i) 'collect and drop off on your way' or (ii) 'collect and bring to the same destination'. In this example, I'm out shopping. On my way home, I'm going to give my brother a ride home the barber shop. pick up = to collect In this example, a package for me has arrived at the post office, and I need to go get it.

blocks.en: Can you pick me up on your way to church?
blocks.def: pick up = to collect (a person). This differs from the 'collect a thing' meaning - as that
blocks.back: means 'collect and bring back' whereas this means either (i) 'collect and drop off on your way' or (ii) 'collect and bring to the same destination'. Here, a friend is asking me if I will drive him / her to church with me.

audios.file: AUDIO Lesson 05.mp3
audios.label: Narração

blocks.en: I want to write a novel but I can't seem to come up with any great storylines.
blocks.def: Come up with = to invent, create, or think of something
blocks.back: I am unable to imagine or create in my mind a clear idea of the story that I want to tell in my new novel.

blocks.en: My daughter has been scouring the Internet trying to come up with some great destination ideas for our upcoming vacation.
blocks.def: Come up with = think of something
blocks.back: My daughter is using the Internet to help her think of or bring to mind good ideas for vacation destinations.

blocks.en: I can't come up with any good reasons not to study a foreign language.
blocks.def: Come up with = think of something
blocks.back: Laziness or lack of motivation are common reasons for not studying a language but I cannot compile in my mind a list of valid reasons why I should not do it.

blocks.en: I hope the creators of this course can continue to come up with more phrasal verb for us to study!
blocks.def: Come up with = Create, remember, think of something
blocks.back: I hope the creative minds at this website can continue to think of or remember many useful phrasal verbs to enhance my knowledge of the English language!

blocks.en: You need to come up with a better excuse than "my dog ate my homework" if you want me to give you more time to complete your assignment.
blocks.def: to come up with = to devise or encounter an excuse
blocks.back: You need to provide me with a better reason for not turning in your assignments than to blame your dog for satiating his craving for your homework.

blocks.en: Brazilian politicians need to come up with a plan to combat corruption in government.
blocks.def: to come up with = to devise or encounter a solution.
blocks.back: Leadership in Brazilian government needs to devise a plan for fighting corruption.

blocks.en: I have only five minutes to come up with the correct answer.
blocks.def: To come up with = to devise or encounter a solution
blocks.back: Time is running out for me to encounter the correct solution to this problem.

blocks.en: I am overweight, so I'm going to hire a dietitian to help me come up with a better dietary plan.
blocks.def: to come up with = to devise, create or encounter a solution.
blocks.back: To combat my obesity, I am going to employ a dietitian to help me devise better ways of feeding myself and planning meals.

blocks.en: If I can't come up with enough money by Friday to pay the light bill, they will cut our electricity.
blocks.def: Come up with = to gather together items or ideas
blocks.back: I need to bring together or gather enough money to get this bill paid so that service is not discontinued.

blocks.en: My sister and brother-in-law are expecting a baby this summer and are trying to come up with some unusual but classy names.
blocks.def: Come up with = to gather together items or ideas
blocks.back: These expectant parents are accumulating lists of ideas for names for their baby.

blocks.en: I get along really well with all of my relatives, thank goodness!
blocks.def: To get along = to live with or interact with others in a peaceful, harmonious way
blocks.back: The relationships I have with my family members are cooperative and peaceful and pleasant. We interact in a courteous and respectful way with each other.

blocks.en: I have one coworker that I can't get along with because he always wants to argue about politics.
blocks.def: To get along = to live with or interact with others in a peaceful, harmonious way
blocks.back: This guy that I work with can't seem to avoid discussing politics with me in an adversarial way and therefore we have a hard time being cordial and pleasant with each other.

blocks.en: My son gets in trouble a lot at school because he has a hard time getting along with the other students.
blocks.def: To get along = to live with or interact with others in a peaceful, harmonious way
blocks.back: Because my son finds it very hard to be pleasant and tolerant and cooperative with the other kids at school, he is often being disciplined by the teachers and administrators.

blocks.en: My next-door neighbor Richard is a crotchety old coot who doesn't get along with any of his neighbors.
blocks.def: To get along = to live with or interact with others in a peaceful, harmonious way
blocks.back: Richard is a grumpy, sour old man who apparently finds it impossible to be neighborly and pleasant with the people who live in his neighborhood.

blocks.en: I'm a simple person, and I can easily get along with just the basic necessities in life.
blocks.def: To get along = to manage to live or survive or even thrive
blocks.back: I'm a person who can be very happy surviving on just the basic things that are necessary for living. I don't need a lot of stuff to be happy.

blocks.en: She was getting along well in school in spite of how busy she was with so many extracurricular activities.
blocks.def: To get along = to manage to live or survive or even thrive
blocks.back: She was managing to be successful in her academics at school even though she was busy with many extra activities such as sports and music.

blocks.en: I am getting along really well in my new job now that I have completed my training.
blocks.def: To get along = to manage to live or survive or even thrive
blocks.back: I have learned all the basic things I need to know to do my job well and now I am having success in my new position.

blocks.en: I couldn't get along without all the help and encouragement my wife gives me.
blocks.def: To get along = to manage to live or survive or even thrive
blocks.back: I couldn't handle everything that I need to every day and thrive in life without the continual support of my wife.

blocks.en: You'd better be getting along now! Your plane is leaving in just three hours.
blocks.def: To get along = to leave or go away from a place
blocks.back: You need to get your things together and head straight for the airport. You need to now leave here and quickly go there because the plane will leave in three hours.

blocks.en: Jessica Tandy was getting along in years before she finally won an Oscar.
blocks.def: To get along in years = to reach old age
blocks.back: Jessica Tandy did not win an Oscar until she was already a very old lady.

blocks.en: I'm really looking forward to returning to Rio next January to show my daughter all the great attractions and natural wonders!
blocks.def: To look forward to = to anticipate something that will happen in the future with happiness
blocks.back: or excitement I'm excited about being able to show my daughter all the places that I have enjoyed visiting in Rio in the past.

blocks.en: I'm not looking forward to getting all four of my wisdom teeth pulled.
blocks.def: To look forward to = to anticipate something that will happen in the future with happiness
blocks.back: or excitement Dental work gives me a lot of anxiety so I am not excited about the prospect of having four teeth removed from my mouth.

blocks.en: Sometimes people get really depressed when they don't have anything fun or exciting to look forward to.
blocks.def: To look forward to = to anticipate something that will happen in the future with happiness
blocks.back: or excitement When people have nothing on the horizon or in the future that gives them a sense of happy expectation or purpose they often will feel depressed.

blocks.en: There's nothing that little kids look forward to with more excitement than opening presents.
blocks.def: To look forward to = to anticipate something that will happen in the future with happiness
blocks.back: or excitement The expectation and mystery connected with imagining what is inside that present creates a lot of excitement in children.

blocks.en: We look forward to seeing you at the fish fry next weekend.
blocks.def: To look forward to = to anticipate something that will happen in the future with happiness
blocks.back: or excitement It makes us happy to know that we will see you at the fish fry this weekend.

blocks.en: If a young person dedicates himself to getting a solid education, he can look forward to a secure future.
blocks.def: To look forward to = to anticipate something that will happen in the future with happiness
blocks.back: or excitement If a young person gets a good education, then they have laid a solid foundation for their future and therefore can anticipate the future with a sense of security and tranquility.

blocks.en: Young people often look forward to growing older, and old people often wish they could be young again.
blocks.def: To look forward to = to anticipate something that will happen in the future with happiness
blocks.back: or excitement Young people very often think that being older will be better and therefore they are excited and are eager for that time to come.

blocks.en: I look forward to the day that I can say that I'm truly fluent in Portuguese.
blocks.def: To look forward to = to anticipate something that will happen in the future with happiness
blocks.back: or excitement The prospect that all of my studying will pay off and that one day I will be able to communicate well in Portuguese gives me a sense of happiness and motivation.

blocks.en: Even though I'm not exactly looking forward to growing older, I know that the golden years certainly offer certain advantages.
blocks.def: To look forward to = to anticipate something that will happen in the future with happiness
blocks.back: or excitement I know that the years at the end of life can be filled with many blessings but I am happy being middle-aged and therefore I am not particularly eager for these years to pass and old age to be upon me.

blocks.en: Every week I look forward to creating a new lesson for my intelligent and dedicated students.
blocks.def: To look forward to = to anticipate something that will happen in the future with happiness
blocks.back: or excitement At the beginning of the week I'm happy to think about the fact that I will have a chance to create a product that will be useful to the people who are depending on me to teach them English!

audios.file: AUDIO - Lesson 06.mp3
audios.label: Narração

blocks.en: Keep on practicing and before you know it, you'll be a soccer star!
blocks.def: keep on = to continue doing something or to do something many times
blocks.back: The word "keep" means to stay in a particular state or to maintain something. "On" carries a sense of forward movement. So in the phrasal verb "keep on" there is a lot of psychology. There is the sense of maintaining effort but also of looking forward. A person who can maintain effort while having a vision of success or a positive future is a motivated person.

blocks.en: Keep on trying and you will succeed.
blocks.def: keep on = to continue doing something or to do something many times
blocks.back: Ever heard of the 10 000 hour principle? Well-known psychology writer Malcolm Gladwell popularized the concept that one needs to spend 10 000 hours on something in order to become a master at it. So the gist of the sample sentence is to keep on doing something until you master it.

blocks.en: "Keep on walking, son. Don't give up. When the going gets tough, the tough get going."
blocks.def: keep on = to continue doing something or to do something many times
blocks.back: Yeah, so do you see the dad taking his son on a wilderness trip to make a man of him? I do.

blocks.en: Why do you keep him on despite his bad attitude?
blocks.def: to keep on = to continue employing someone
blocks.back: So this employee thinks he is God's gift to the workplace. He is arrogant, thinks he knows better than anyone else and has shockingly bad relationships with his colleagues. So why does the boss keep him on? Let's find out.

blocks.en: I keep him on because he is a technical genius. There isn't a computer he cannot fix!
blocks.def: to keep on = to continue employing someone
blocks.back: So that's the reason the boss keeps him on. The guy may not be great with people but he is superb with computers.

blocks.en: The boss only keeps her on because she wears skimpy tops and tight jeans, or so the gossip goes.
blocks.def: to keep on = to continue employing someone
blocks.back: The girl in this sample sentence is not kept on because she is a computer whiz. But she has other skills…

blocks.en: My daughter keeps on and on about how bad her skin is and how she needs ruaccutan.
blocks.def: keep on = to talk continuously about something or to repeat something many times in an
blocks.back: annoying way So this daughter is putting a lot of pressure on her mom to let her use the medication. Notice how the preposition "on" is repeated: keeps on and on. The repetition suggests the irritation that the mother feels.

blocks.en: My mother-in-law keeps on and on about how lucky I was to marry her son.
blocks.def: keep on = to talk continuously about something or to repeat something many times in an
blocks.back: annoying way Sub-text: this mother-in-law is not happy with her daughter-in-law. The irritation that the daughter-in-law feels with the mother-in-law is clear in her use of the phrasal verb "keeps on and on".

blocks.en: The famous writer CS Lewis made up an imaginary country with his older brother Warren. They called it Boxen and made up a 400-year old history for Boxen. Now that's what I call imagination!
blocks.def: make up = to invent a story
blocks.back: If you were lucky enough to read The Chronicles of Narnia you will remember the amazing ability that CS Lewis had to make things up - the fantasy world of Narnia is populated with mythical beasts, evil witches and handsome princes. The power of Lewis's imagination, his ability to make things up, has touched the lives of millions of children and adults alike!

blocks.en: My dad did not plan much in his life. He made it up as he went along.
blocks.def: make up = to improvise
blocks.back: This family probably ran into a few scrapes because the dad did not plan much but he lived intuitively and spontaneously. He did not follow a rule book.

blocks.en: I do not have a specific itinerary for my world trip; I'll make it up as I go. Whatever moves me!
blocks.def: make up = to improvise
blocks.back: So next week this guy could be in Guarujá, Guangzhou, Glasgow, or Grand Rapids. Who knows! He'll improvise as he goes.

blocks.en: In the last few months of his life the cancer patient tried to make up for broken relationships and lost opportunities
blocks.def: Make up = compensate
blocks.back: Doctors who understand terminal care - that is care for those who are dying - know that one of the most important things to do before a terminal patient dies, is to address any unresolved relationship problems. Reconciliation with family members with whom one has had difficult relationships is tremendously comforting for both patient and loved one.

blocks.en: Here is a make-up tip: when you make up your eyes, always apply the pencil to the upper part of the brow to give the illusion of lift.
blocks.def: make up = put cosmetics on your face
blocks.back: It is important to distinguish between the phrasal verb "make up" and the noun "make-up". The next sample sentence will explain the difference.

blocks.en: Women use make-up to make up their faces.
blocks.def: make up = put cosmetics on your face
blocks.back: Women use make-up (noun) to make up (phrasal verb) their faces.

blocks.en: I have made up my mind. You are not moving into a flat next year. You will stay in res for another year. It is cheaper and safer.
blocks.def: make up = decide
blocks.back: This father has made up his mind - he has decided on a certain course of action and is not likely to change his mind. As long as he pays for his daughter's university education he is not going to allow her to move into a flat by herself.

blocks.en: The best part of a fight is what happens afterwards when you make up!
blocks.def: make up = be reconciled after a quarrel
blocks.back: I won't go into the details!

blocks.en: The rescue team is made up of three people: an experienced mountaineer, a tracker and a doctor.
blocks.def: make up = consist of
blocks.back: In this case make up refers to different parts that are part of the whole. The whole is the rescue party. The parts are the experienced mountaineer, the tracker and the doctor. Together these "parts" make up, or form, the whole. The whole is made up of or consists of the three parts.

blocks.en: We have to make up the pages before we can go to the printer.
blocks.def: make up = prepare for printing
blocks.back: In the magazine and newspaper business pages have to be made up before they can be printed. In other words, the design and layout and wording all have to be put together perfectly before printing can begin.

blocks.en: The golden rule is: back up your computer files every day.
blocks.def: back up = to make a copy of
blocks.back: To back up means to make a copy. Computer crashes always happen when you least expect it or when you can least afford to lose the work you have done - like half an hour before the most important presentation of your life. The same goes for computer viruses. Once that worm has penetrated your system and rendered everything gibberish, it is too late to back up your work.

blocks.en: I have no sympathy for you. I told you repeatedly to back up your doctoral thesis and you were too lazy to do so. Now you have lost three months' work!
blocks.def: back up = to make a copy of
blocks.back: I FEEL for this student. But to be honest, anyone who spends months writing a doctoral thesis without taking the precaution to back it up, does not deserve an advanced degree!

blocks.en: Will you back me up if I speak out against crime in this area?
blocks.def: back up = to support
blocks.back: People are often afraid to speak their minds in public about important issues, but having someone who backs you up, who supports you, always helps.

blocks.en: Will you back up my story if I tell my wife that we didn't take a detour via the pub?
blocks.def: back up = to support
blocks.back: So this is a different kind of support. Not the good kind necessarily. But what do they say about strength in numbers? The more sincerely his buddies back up, support, his story, the more likely the guy's wife is to believe him.

blocks.en: Will the United Nations back up its verbal criticism of the dictatorship with real action?
blocks.def: back up = to support
blocks.back: There are idioms for this sort of thing. "Talk is cheap and actions speak louder than words." So very often in international politics threats don't help. They have to be backed up or supported by action - usually of the military kind.

blocks.en: The best approach to writing good argumentative essays is to back up all your arguments with sound research.
blocks.def: back up = to prove that something is right
blocks.back: Yes, backing up your arguments in an argumentative essay is crucial. Make sure the sources you quote are reliable, though. It is no use backing up an argument by referring to unreliable or erroneous statistics!

blocks.en: The highway was backed up for miles after two furniture removal trucks had collided. Lounge suits, mattresses and dining room tables were strewn everywhere.
blocks.def: back up = to pile up
blocks.back: I am sure you can imagine the miles and miles of piled up, backed up, cars and the hundreds of impatient drivers drumming their fingers on their steering wheels and the poor furniture removals guys frantically trying to salvage what is left of their clients' household contents.

blocks.en: Could you back up a bit so I can get my trolley out of the lift before you take occupation?
blocks.def: back up = to make a person or a thing go backwards
blocks.back: So here is the scenario: The lift is jam-packed. It smells of humans and you can't wait to get out with your trolley, laden with summer sale bargains. When the doors open, though, the people waiting to enter the lift surge forward like a stampede of angry cattle and you are half-trapped between the lift and the impatient cows … people, I mean. That's when you ask them to back up - to move backwards.

blocks.en: Could you please back up a bit so I can get out of the parking spot?
blocks.def: back up = to make a person or a thing go backwards
blocks.back: This scenario is similar to the trolley example I have just given you. This time we are talking cars instead of trolleys. You're trying to get out of the parking space but the guy who is eyeing your parking spot is so eager to claim his territory that he leaves you no space for maneuvering out of what has, after all, been your spot for the last two hours. That's when you give him the "back up" wave.

blocks.en: ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE Hi, this is Melissa Faulkner, coming to you from Durham, North Carolina.
Today we are going to talk about three phrasal verbs - 'fall apart', 'put up with' and 'pass out'.
Now for each phrasal verb, I'm going to give you three sentences.
We'll talk about how to use those three phrasal verbs in a sentence, with a short explanation.
So let's go ahead and get started with the first phrasal verb.
Now, 'fall apart' has two kind of different meanings, one of them is literal and one of them is figurative.
So the first version of 'fall apart' is a material.
Sort of when a material starts to break up or disintegrate, when it starts to come apart, we would say that it's falling apart.
Now the more figurative version of this verbal phrase 'fall apart' is when sort of an idea or a plan starts to fall apart.
It starts to become disorganized or it starts to go differently than you expected it to go.
So let's get started with sentence number one: The bread on the sandwich was soaked with mayonnaise and it soon began to fall apart.
So in this case, to 'fall apart' means that a material or something physical is falling apart.
So in this case, there is mayonnaise on the sandwich, so mayonnaise is a sauce.
The sauce is making the bread sort of soft and it's causing the bread to fall apart, to come apart or to break.
So when you are eating the sandwich, sort of its soaked in sauce, and it becomes very difficult to eat because the bread is sort of coming apart.
Let's move on to sentence number two: After the visiting team scored 10 runs in the seventh inning, the home team began to fall apart.
Now, this is that second version of the phrase 'fall apart'.
It is the more figurative version of 'fall apart'.
So this means that the team was becoming disorganized or ineffective.
So when the visiting team came, they scored 10 points, they scored 10 runs in the seventh inning and the home team started to get discouraged.
They maybe didn't catch the ball as well; they weren't hitting as well.
They were falling apart or becoming disorganized as a team.
Let's move on to sentence number 3: Jeff's old wooden fishing boat had been in the family for over 30 years and the water damage was causing it to fall apart.
So in this case, 'fall apart' means to break apart or to disintegrate.
So you can imagine that this boat has been around for 30 years.
It's probably been on a dock somewhere, in the water for all that time.
The water is starting to make the wood come apart or break apart so the fishing boat is starting to fall apart.
It's not as good as it once was.
Let's move on to the second phrasal verb 'put up with'.

Now 'put up with' means when there is a situation that's sort of unpleasant or not a great situation, but even though it's not a great situation, you are patient and you decide to accept that situation as best you can, so you 'put up with' the situation.
So let's go on to sentence number 1: Alison couldn't put up with her boss' mean comments about her weight any longer.
So in this case, Alison has a boss.

He has maybe been making some mean comments about her weight, maybe how she needs to lose some weight and she's been patient for a really long time because it's her boss and she doesn't want to lose her job.
But at this point, he's been giving these mean comments for such a long time that she's just getting tired of it.
She just can't put up with it anymore.
Maybe she's going to say something to him, maybe she is even going to quit, but she can't put up with it anymore.
Let's go on to sentence number 2: Caleb has to put up with how slow his computer is because he doesn't want to spend money on a new one right now.
So in this situation, Caleb's computer is really slow.
Maybe he's trying to write a document or do some work on his computer and it's taking forever to load or to save and it's really annoying.
But he doesn't want to buy a new computer right now.
He doesn't want to spend any money.
So, he is patient with his computer.
He decides to put up with the fact that his computer is so slow so that he doesn't have to buy a new one.
Even though Jaylin is a procrastinator, Mr. Jones puts up with it because Jaylin always turns in excellent writing.
Now in this situation, Jaylin is a procrastinator.
A procrastinator is someone who doesn't turn in their work on time or waits until the very last minute to turn their work in.
So Mr. Jones normally would punish Jaylin because he's either turning his work in late or he's turning it in right at the last minute.

But Mr. Jones decides to put up with it, he decides to be patient with Jaylin because every time Jaylin does turn in his work, it's really awesome, it is excellent work, so he decides to put up with it.
Let's move on to our third phrasal verb - 'pass out'.
Now there are two different versions of the phrase 'pass out'.
The first version means when you're passing something out, it means that you're giving out multiple items.
So maybe there's a group and you are giving out things to the group.
Maybe you have a lot of items and you're giving them out or you're passing them out.
The second version, 'to pass out' means to faint or to fall down.

So when someone has a medical condition, maybe they're feeling lightheaded or they're feeling a little sick and they sort of go unconscious for a second and fall down to the ground, we would call that passing out.
So let's start with sentence number 1: Mrs. Rose wanted to pass out lollipops to her students but they were being extremely disrespectful, so she kept them in her bag.
In this case, Mrs. Rose is probably a teacher.
She has a group of students.
She has a bag of lollipops.
She wants to give each of her students a lollipop.
She is going to pass out the lollipops.
But in this case, they are being a little disrespectful so she decides not to.
But she would have originally passed out or given out her lollipops to her students.
Sentence number 2: I woke up at 4 o'clock AM to go to the sale at Walmart because they were passing out 100 coupons for a free refrigerator.
So in this case, Walmart is having a sale.
They have 100 coupons and the first 100 people to come, get a coupon for a free refrigerator.

So in this case, the buyer, the person in the sentence, is going to get up really early to make sure that they are in line to be one of the first 100 people because Walmart is passing out coupons and so they want to get one of those coupons to get a free refrigerator.
Let's take a look at sentence number 3: When Laura saw the stitches on the bottom of Jacob's foot, she felt sick to her stomach and then she eventually passed out.
So this is that second version of the phrase 'pass out'.
It means to medically go unconscious.
So Laura looked at Jacob's foot, it had stitches on it, maybe it looked really gross.
Laura doesn't like looking at gross things and so her stomach starts to feel bad and then eventually she passes out.
Somebody has to help wake her up or they have to call the ER or something like that.
Those are our three phrasal verbs for this time.
I hope these explanations were helpful to you and I hope I get the chance to talk to you about some other phrasal verbs in the future.
